citation.title: Algorithm Aversion Towards AI-Generated Multiple-Choice Questions

reading.source_scope_note: Medical students answered/rated actual human- and GPT4o-authored MCQs under two source labels. Item allocation/order was randomized within fixed human-labelled-first and AI-labelled-second blocks, leaving label/order confounding. The testing effect is defined from earlier memory literature, not measured longitudinally here.
access_limits: All nine extracted pages read, including participant flow, exact rating items, model specifications, tables, limitations and references. Figure2 visually checked for the difficulty-direction error and exact plotted means.

External prompts/items, supplementary instruments, raw rating dataset and R code were not independently obtained. The original testing-effect papers were not read, and no retained-learning outcome was reproduced.

study.origins: 20human-authored,20GPT4o-generated, based on20topics; all in German, AI items checked for accuracy without difficulty revision
study.assignment: Random items to blocks and randomized order within each; no reported counterbalancing of block labels or same-item label crossover across participants
study.responses: Five-option single-best-answer; relevance and wording ratings1–7 after each item
study.moderators: Self-reportedAI literacy and attitudes; LLM experience omitted from models after fit/convergence problems
study.analysis: CLMMs with subject random intercept only; actual-origin term dropped from moderator models due convergence issues

summary: The study reports lower wording ratings in the AI-labelled block despite high ratings overall, but fixed block order and unmodeled item differences limit a clean causal anti-AI interpretation. Add the explicitly defined testing effect as a secondary human memory construct; retain its distinction from immediate quiz success and model self-testing.

findings.origin: Cognitive psychology / learning and retrieval practice
findings.definition: Improved later retention of learned material following active retrieval in a test.
findings.novelty_rationale: A retrieval-based learning benefit, distinct from mere repetition, exposure-driven familiarity, retrieval cue specificity or a generator's ability to answer an exam question. Taking a test is the procedure; improved subsequent retention is the effect.

evidence.quote: improves the long-term retention of the materials

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction defines the effect through Roediger/Karpicke2006 and discusses testing as a learning tool. The present experiment measures immediate MCQ accuracy and ratings, not delayed retention or a retrieval-versus-restudy control. Original memory studies remain unread.
findings.boundary: Higher immediate accuracy, easier questions or repeated answer production do not establish improved later memory. The effect depends on material, retrieval success, feedback and comparison condition. An inference-only language model does not acquire human memory simply by generating answers; any AI analogue needs a persistent learning/memory mechanism and separate delayed evaluation.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human learning effect defined secondarily; no delayed human retention test or model learning mechanism measured in this paper
findings.ai_proposal: For people, compare retrieval practice with matched study time and test delayed retention/transfer. For systems with persistent memory or explicit updates, compare active retrieval against matched exposure on held-out later tasks; distinguish in-context rehearsal, storage and weight changes, and guard against evaluation leakage.

findings.term: Lower wording ratings associated with an AI-labelled MCQ block
findings.definition: Students rated wording less favourably in the block labelled AI-generated, regardless of actual question origin, while actual AI questions were easier and received higher relevance ratings.
findings.novelty_rationale: A reported human source-label evaluation pattern for an existing construct; no duplicateanti-AI-biasID and no claim the blocked design cleanly isolates the label effect.
findings.evidence_scope: 145students,40items each; wordingCLMMlabelb−.55,SE.07,z−7.45,p<.001,OR.57. Plotted wordingmeans5.81/5.82firsthumanlabel versus5.46/5.44secondAIlabel. The label is confounded with block/time and fixed item subsets; model random effects include students only.
findings.boundary: A source-label association is not proof of irrational aversion or lower actual quality, and fixed-order fatigue/context effects remain plausible. High ratings make practical importance modest; no measured refusal to use learning materials or worse learning follows. Source origin, stated label, item difficulty and position should be independently varied.

findings.term: Easier items rated more relevant does not by itself demonstrate a halo mechanism
findings.definition: The authors propose that easier AI-generated questions seemed less threatening and therefore received higher relevance ratings, but ease, self-esteem and a causal spillover were not independently manipulated.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retains a hypothesized explanation separately from demonstrated output/evaluation effects rather than counting it as another established halo experiment.
findings.evidence_scope: ActualAIitems77%correctversushuman48%; relevance means5.96–6.00versushuman5.64–5.85 dependinglabel. No direct self-esteem/threat measure or matched-difficulty comparison isolates spillover.
findings.boundary: Question difficulty can legitimately affect suitability for formative preparation. A relevance difference need not be an irrelevant-quality halo effect. Test independent wording quality or another outcome while matching objective learning requirements; do not infer threatened self-esteem solely from ratings.

methodological_limits: 145of380invited students volunteered for an optional formative session at one university. Self-selection and narrow language/curriculum limit population and high-stakes generalization.
145participated whileTable1uses140complete instrument responses and134LLMexperience responses. These distinct denominators are explicit, not evidence of one common complete sample.

The human-labelled block is always first and AI-labelled block second. Randomizing items within blocks and their origin allocation does not randomize/counterbalance label order; fatigue, practice and contrast are confounded with source label.
No reported same-item crossover places identical content under both labels across participants. Thus labels also attach to different fixed item subsets.

CLMMs use a participant random intercept but no item/topic random effect or participant label slope. Repeated ratings over40fixeditems do not provide5800independent randomized source-label assignments.
Item generation is based on matched broad topics, not matched wording, difficulty, specificity or cognitive demand. AIitems are easier, and both difficulty and content can affect relevance.
An expert verified AI item correctness, but no independent blinded item-quality panel or systematic learner-target validation was reported.
GPT4ois named without a pinned snapshot or complete inference settings in the main article. Externalgenerationprompt/fullitems were not obtained; no universal claim about AI question quality follows.
Immediate proportion-correct is an item easiness index under the method, not a delayed retention or clinical reasoning score.

Figure2caption reverses difficulty direction: it says0meansallcorrectand1meansnonecorrect, while methods defineproportioncorrectand plotted .53/.43human versus .80/.74AI average to the reported48%/77%. The plotted data align with the methods/results, not the caption's definition.
No detected discrimination differenceU225,p.51 is not formal equivalence or proof equal psychometric quality. Only20itemsperactualorigin, shared students and limited item range constrain comparison.
Discrimination coefficients depend on item easiness and the particular test/sample; two similar mean coefficients do not establish equivalent content coverage or educational validity.
Relevance and wording ratings are near the ceiling: means5.44–6.00on1–7, many6/7. A statistically detectable latent odds difference need not cause meaningful adoption or learning consequences.

The reportedorigin×labelinteraction forrelevance cannot be reduced to a simple uniform label effect without estimated marginal contrasts. Some prose simplifies the interaction and no full coefficient table was independently inspected.
Moderator models omit actualorigin because of convergence problems. They answer a changed/partially adjusted question and can inherit item-origin confounding.
LLMexperience is removed from inferential models after convergence/fit problems; null results for other self-reports do not establish experience is irrelevant.
AI literacy and attitudes are self-reported after the examination, not objective competence tests or randomized traits. Accuracy of self-appraisal and possible task effects remain unknown.
Page2950reportsattitudesrelevanceb.01,SE.13,z.05,p.096. A conventionaltwo-sidedz.05test givespabout.96; the displayed statistics need reconciliation rather than treatingp.096asexact.
Methods cite reference14forSNAIL, but reference14is Raupach's2016test-enhancedlearning trial rather than a scale-validation source. Exact instrument provenance should be checked in the supplement.

Some wording-model paragraphs copy relevance labels into outcome/missingness descriptions. The stated5616wordingratings/184missing and other model-specific counts should be verified against raw output.
Main and interaction nulls do not prove no moderation, equality across sources or actual political/technological neutrality. Ceiling and model-fit limits reduce power.
Self-esteem threat, social desirability and cognitive-load explanations are proposed, not measured mediators. Easier items may legitimately be more useful for a particular learner.
No long-term learning, transfer, actual use/adoption or summative exam consequences were measured. The testing effect is discussed secondarily rather than demonstrated.
The dataavailabilitysentenceendswith canbeobtainedbythecorrespondingauthorupon in the suppliedPDF. Rawdata/Rcode and supplementary instruments were not retrieved.
Theoretical source names in the bibliography do not count as separately read primary studies; source corrections are retained without silently revising reported outcomes.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Hayden's clinical ranking improvement and Laupichler's easier quiz performance are immediate outcomes, not durable skill acquisition or testing-effect evidence. Measure the outcome actually claimed.

Heßler studies stated support preference under randomized context; Laupichler's apparent source aversion uses fixed-order blocks. Their control quality differs and pooled causal aversion claims require care.
Banks' fixed progression likewise mixes specificity with order and prompting. Calling a sequence a within-subject design does not isolate the psychological factor of interest.

deferred.term: Anti-AI bias as a new behaviour
deferred.reason: Already covered by algorithm-aversion for this source-label devaluation. No new ID for a near-synonym.
A plausible post hoc explanation without a direct self-esteem measure or matched-difficulty manipulation.

deferred.term: AI literacy as a protective mechanism
deferred.reason: No significant moderation and no causal intervention; a self-report score is not a demonstrated behaviour or mitigation.
Different studies use different item sets, topics and versions; no controlled longitudinal model capability comparison here.

limitations: One explicitly secondary human memory effect added; no delayed-learning or AI-training claim.
Existing aversion evidence retained with major label/order/item confounds and practical-effect limits; halo explanation remains a noncorroborating reference.
